newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia condemns NATO "cowboy raids" in Bosnia.
newsitem.headline: Russia condemns NATO "cowboy raids" in Bosnia.

text.p: Russia on Friday denounced NATO's sudden swoop on Bosnian Serb war crimes suspects as "cowboy raids" which threatened the Dayton peace process.
"Russia does not bear and does not intend to bear any responsibility for the consequences of such unilateral actions," a Foreign Ministry statement said.
"One must underline that such 'cowboy raids' threaten the whole Dayton Peace process."
The statement hinted that Russia might review the participation of its troops in the international SFOR peacekeeping force in Bosnia.
"The Russian leadership will draw the corresponding conclusions from this," it said.

The tough wording might indicate the worst disagreement between Russia and NATO over Bosnia since September 1995, when the Western defence alliance launched air strikes against Bosnian Serb military targets around Sarajevo.

But the statement also seemed intended to appease President Boris Yeltsin's nationalist and communist critics who have accused him and the government of doing too little to stand up to the West and defend Russia's fellow Orthodox Christian Slavs, the Serbs, in Bosnia.

British special forces arrested one suspect and shot dead another on Thursday in the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation's first operation against indicted war criminals since a Bosnia peace treaty was signed in Dayton, Ohio in 1995.
U.S. President Bill Clinton defended the offensive as "the right thing to do" during a visit to Bucharest on Friday.
Russian deputy prime minister Valery Serov hailed improving relations with NATO at a news conference in Moscow but regretted Thursday's war-criminal operation.
"We categorically condemn what has happened in Bosnia and do not share that approach," Serov said.

The Russian Foreign Ministry statement said Thursday's action had overstepped the peacekeepers' mandate, and that any decision on arrests should be made through direct cooperation between the parties to the U.N. warcrimes tribunal in The Hague.
"We have repeatedly stressed that we support the just punishment of all those guilty of war crimes in Bosnia-Herzegovina," the Foreign Ministry said.
"However the arrest of suspects does not correspond to the mandate of the international force deployed in Bosnia."
Tensions over international policy in Bosnia have surfaced periodically since the conflict erupted in 1992, due to Moscow's sympathies for the Serbs.

Russia's relations with NATO and its four partners in the five-nation contact group on former Yugoslavia -- France, Germany, Britain and the United States -- became particularly difficult during the NATO air strikes of 1995.
A Russian government statement at that time said the present generation of Bosnian Serbs was "threatened by genocide".
But the differences were patched up as the peace process gathered momentum and relations have been more stable since the Dayton peace treaty was signed.
Western leaders have praised Russia's part in the international peacekeeping effort in Bosnia as a model of cooperation between former Cold War enemies.
